title: Role of Interfacial Coherency on Creep Behavior of FCC/BCC High-Entropy Alloy Multilayers.

recollection.starting_material: Guess: Magnetron-sputtered nanoscale multilayers composed of an FCC high-entropy alloy (e.g., CoCrNi or CoCrFeMnNi) alternating with a BCC refractory HEA (e.g., NbMoTaW or VNbMoTa), with bilayer thicknesses on the order of 5–50 nm deposited on a crystalline substrate to control orientation relationships.
recollection.intervention: Guess: Interfacial coherency was tuned by adjusting lattice misfit via composition (and/or deposition temperature) and by post-annealing to promote or disrupt coherency, producing coherent, semi-coherent, and incoherent FCC/BCC interfaces. Creep behavior was probed via high-temperature nanoindentation or micropillar compression (≈500–700 °C, ~25–300 MPa) while systematically varying bilayer thickness.
recollection.structure: Guess: Alternating FCC/BCC nanoscale multilayers exhibiting: (i) coherent interfaces with Kurdjumov–Sachs/Nishiyama–Wassermann-type orientation relationships; (ii) semi-coherent interfaces with periodic misfit dislocation networks; and (iii) incoherent interfaces with limited registry and interfacial disorder. HRTEM/STEM showed sharp interfaces, periodic misfit dislocations for semi-coherent cases, and columnar grains; residual coherency strain fields were observed in the coherent stacks.
recollection.mechanism: Guess: Coherent interfaces suppress interfacial sliding and fast diffusion, shifting creep to dislocation climb and lattice diffusion within the layers (higher stress exponent and activation energy). Incoherent interfaces provide fast-diffusion paths and permit interfacial/grain-boundary-like sliding (Coble/interface-controlled creep), yielding lower stress exponents and activation energies. Increasing interface area (thinner layers) magnifies these effects, with coherent stacks remaining barrier-controlled and incoherent stacks becoming interface-diffusion dominated.
recollection.results: Guess: Coherent interfaces reduced steady-state creep rates by 1–2 orders of magnitude compared to incoherent interfaces across the tested temperatures. score.note: The recollection is largely speculative. It incorrectly describes coherency as tuned by composition, temperature, or annealing rather than by layer thickness (8–80 nm) during sputtering. It generically recognizes coherent, semicoherent, and incoherent interfaces and correctly associates semicoherent interfaces with misfit dislocations, but misses the actual grain-boundary dominance at larger periods. The proposed mechanism is reversed: the paper finds semicoherent M16 most creep-resistant and invokes pileups followed by interfacial amorphization-mediated diffusion/slip, whereas coherent interfaces transmit dislocations more readily. The stated temperatures, stresses, creep rates, activation energies, and stress exponents do not match the reported nanoindentation results.
